all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

defining_facts.text: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular.
Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.

The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements.
The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.
A well-planned contextual inquiry process generally takes one to two hours.

Observations and interaction with users in contextual inquiry enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace, which supports design decisions.

Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting, reveals their unique behavioral traits, and enables design refinement; without it, designers may create invalid designs and give essential user activities equal importance to unnecessary features, compromising usability.

User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group.
Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement-gathering method that observes targeted or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.
The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.

The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data.

The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.
The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.
The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does.

Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.
Contextual inquiry is one of many methods available for usability requirement gathering.

never_defined.definition: The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

never_defined.name: class note-taking application
never_defined.definition: In the class note-taking application example, the 19 affinity-diagram ideas are organized into six groups with the headers navigation in notebook, media content, navigation in notes, note organization, text formatting, and storage and privacy, containing 3, 5, 2, 2, 4, and 3 ideas respectively.

never_defined.name: header
never_defined.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

never_defined.name: reminder setting
never_defined.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

never_defined.name: work scheduling
never_defined.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.
